# Queueing tasks Writing a task (Queueing tasks), deferring it, asking the user to queue it, and linking, placing and ordering it. Grooming one, whether you write it, start it or groom ungroomed Backlog tasks, is in [groom.md](groom.md). Ordering is the user's (see Positions). ## Do, queue or drop When you notice something beyond what the task's After says, choose one: - **Do it in the task** when the After needs it, or when it is a small fix in code the task already changes. - **Queue it** only when it is in another unit (project), needs its own approval, or is unrelated to the goal. - **Drop it** when you would not bother doing it yourself. Do not queue or offer it. ## Queueing tasks When something you chose to queue comes up, queue it as a task and move on: its subject and what you know. `splates task add` puts it in a lane, which says you groomed it: you checked no task already asks it, linked what blocks it, and put it in a lane (`--lane`, Backlog when none is plain; see [groom.md](groom.md)). When you know too little of it to do that without looking into it, as for a rough idea or a request deferred as it came, `splates task defer` it instead, which takes the same flags and leaves it in Backlog, ungroomed, for whoever grooms it. Leave its position to the user and the queue, unless the user names it. Leave its model off too, unless the user names one: a task that names none goes to Auto pick, which judges its words and starts it on the agent, model and thinking level the user's rules give. Give each task a `--slug`: a short lowercase-with-dashes name for what it changes, a few words such as `upload-413`, never the subject cut short. The task that takes it starts under that name, and its branch, worktree and conversation carry it. Give each task its tag with `--tag ` when the config lists tags (`splates task update --tag ` adds one later), and leave the project's name out of the subject and the slug: the tag says it. Write a task's subject short enough to scan. Write its detail with both `## Before` and `## After`, never just After, the shape a task record has, as markdown the `splates server` page renders. Each is a line and a picture, as text alone rarely shows the change (a real screenshot of today's screen or a D2 diagram of today's flow for Before, `splates attach`ed; a lo-fi mock or D2 diagram for After). Before is always there: for a new thing it says what exists today in its place (that there is nothing yet, or what the user does instead). Leave the picture out only for a trivial change or when you have not looked at the code yet, for the agent that takes it to add. After is one short paragraph saying what changes, with no lists. Put the why, the where and the files in a `## Details` section after it, with `- [ ]` steps, inline code for paths and commands, and fenced blocks for snippets. Single quotes keep the shell off the backticks: ```sh splates task add "Upload retries forever on a 413" --slug upload-413 '## Before The client retries on any 4xx in `src/upload.ts`, so a 413 loops forever. ## After An upload stops retrying on a 413 and tells the user the file is too big. ## Details - [ ] stop retrying on 413 - [ ] tell the user the file is too big' ``` The `splates server` page shows each `splates task add` in the conversation as a line naming the task, which opens it, so your reply needs no heading or summary of it. That shrinks what you say, never the task: its subject and detail stay full, since whoever picks it up reads nothing else. `splates task update ''` replaces the whole detail, so pass all of it: what still holds and what you learned. ## Taking a queued task When you take a queued task that names a model other than the one you run as, take it anyway: whoever handed it to you chose you. Say so in a line of its own right after `splates add`, such as `#12 names Sonnet; I run as Opus.`, so the user can stop you and start the model it names instead. When `splates add --task` warns that a task is blocked, what blocks it has yet to merge: `splates task wait ` for it, or, when the user asked for this task now, do only what does not need the blocker and say so in your report. When `splates task show` prints a `deferred:` line, the task was set aside before, and the user's Resume on its Deferred card, or the queue, sends it again: check each blocker under it still unticked (an upstream release, a key) before any other work. One that still holds defers it again with `splates remove --reason blocked`, its why saying what you checked and found; once none holds, carry on from its detail. Merging removes the queued task yours took: when you leave part of it undone, `splates task add` what is left as a task of its own. ## Deferring `[SPLATES DEFER]` asks you to make a request a task rather than do it. `splates task defer` it as Queueing tasks says, from your worktree when a task is under way, its detail all the message gives and what you already know of the code it touches, with no new investigation. Sent alone, it defers work you may have begun: save it before you stop. Put what you learned and did on that request since the message in the task's detail, ticking off the `- [ ]` steps done. When you started a task for it, commit what its worktree holds, write in the detail that it carries on there with `splates claim `, and bring `SPLATES.md` up to date, the `## Next` step it came from saying it is deferred to task #N. Either way, take no further step toward the request and reply with nothing beyond the line the page shows for the task; then, after a request, carry on with any work under way, and, sent alone, end your turn. A task of yours deferred with `splates remove --reason blocked` asks the same of its detail, given as `--detail`: why it stopped, what you found, the steps done ticked off, those left, and, since the remove discards the branch, what of it is worth redoing, for a stranger who has none of this conversation. ## Asking the user to queue You never change the queue: splates refuses an agent `splates queue add`, `remove`, `move`, `pause` and `resume`, and `splates lane queue` and `unqueue`. The user queues, from the board or from the queue card your reply ends with. A task is one medium-sized change: one coherent thing you can state in a sentence, that an agent can finish without carrying decisions from an earlier step. When a request is several of those, such as a feature in steps or a list of fixes, or needs a second project, judge that from the request itself, before reading code, and offer a lane rather than do them all here. Ask it as a numbered Yes/No question, naming the tasks it would split into and picking Yes, and do no part of the work until it is answered: ```markdown 1. Should I split this into a lane of three tasks? Smaller tasks land faster and are easier to review: the CSV writer, the endpoint that uses it, and the page's export button. - (a) Yes, add a lane and queue nothing yet (chosen) - (b) No, do all of it in this task ``` On Yes, `splates lane add ''`, named for what they add up to, then `splates task add` each into it, groomed and linked as Lanes says, and `splates remove` the task you started with `--reason superseded` once they are added. On No, do it all in this task, without raising it again and without queuing split points as follow-ups. Leave one change with a follow-up or two to a task and its follow-ups, and do the change itself when the user asked for it, so a request that is one medium change gets no offer. Then end your reply with the lane's queue card, naming it by number, and what the tasks add up to under it: ```markdown ## 🔐 Permission: queue lane 7: Billing export `splates lane queue 7` The CSV writer first, then the endpoint and the page's button that use it. ``` When the user asks you to queue a request for a worker, rather than do it, work out what it wants first: read what you need of the code, and ask each call their answer would change as [questions.md](questions.md) says, ending your turn on them, since whoever starts it reads nothing but the task. Then add it groomed, as Grooming a task you write in [groom.md](groom.md) says, updating an open task that already asks it rather than adding another, and end your reply with its card, naming each task by number: ```markdown ## 🔐 Permission: queue #31, #32: Upload fixes `splates queue add 31 32` Both stop retries the server already refused. ``` Under its title, give the command that queues it, on a line of its own in backticks, so a user reading in a terminal can run it themselves. The `splates server` page lists the work on the card as the board has it, with that command to copy, and Queue now for the user to press; the choice is theirs and reaches only the board, never you. Ask for one queue card a reply, at its end, and leave it at that: whatever the user picks, carry on with any work under way, and do none of the work on the card in this conversation unless they ask you to. ## Changing several units A task changes one unit of the repository, the package or project its After names, so a change that reaches several lands as several tasks, in order, rather than one that touches them all. When a unit's change breaks what another unit takes from it (an export's signature, a schema, a config key), the merge gate fails on the consumer's tests, which is no reason to widen the task. Expand, migrate, contract instead: 1. **Expand.** This task adds the new form beside the old, so every consumer still works, and lands. 2. **Migrate.** One task per consuming unit moves it to the new form, `--blocked-by` the expanding task, so the queue starts them once it merges, in a lane when they are many. 3. **Contract.** A last task removes the old form, `--blocked-by` every migration. Queue steps 2 and 3 before merging step 1, each written as Queueing tasks says, its detail naming the old and new forms and the files it reaches. Only a change that cannot land in steps (a rename the old form cannot survive beside, a format both sides must switch at once) takes one task across units, and then its After names every unit it touches, so the reach is chosen and shown rather than crept into. ## Links When a task cannot start before another merges, it is blocked by that one: say so with `--blocked-by` (`splates task add --blocked-by 12`, or `splates task update 14 --blocked-by 12`), rather than in its detail. splates then warns whoever takes it early, drops the link when 12 merges, and shows it on the board. Once 12 merges, `splates task show 14` names the commit it landed as; if 12 is removed without merging, 14 is held as Blocked for the user, who lets go of the link from its card (the page's remove lists such tasks first). `--remove-blocked-by 12` undoes a link or lets go of a removed blocker. Several links go in one call, the flag repeated or a comma list: `--blocked-by 12 --blocked-by 13`, or `--blocked-by 12,13`. Link only for a real order (one needs the other's code or data), never for priority, which is the position's job. A task that waits on another project's task links it the same way, with that project's slug before the number: `--blocked-by wren#404` (or `'wren #404'`), mixed freely with numbers here. The task there has to be open; when there is none yet, `splates --project wren task defer` it first (see [projects.md](projects.md)). The queue holds this task until that one merges there, and the board, `splates task show` and `splates queue list` name it with where it stands, while `task show` there lists this task under `blocking:`. A blocker removed there without merging holds the task for the user, as one here does; `--remove-blocked-by wren#404` lets go of it. Never leave such a wait only in a task's detail or a deferral's `--waiting-on`: unlinked, the user cannot see what holds the work up. ## Lanes A lane is a named group of related tasks, for the user to see them together on the board. Every lane is on exactly one board (see Boards below). It orders nothing: the queue starts tasks, and links alone say what must land first, so link a task `--blocked-by` another whenever it needs that one's code or changes its files, even in the same lane. A lane has no model of its own: each task names its own, or Auto pick picks it. Placing a task, read `splates lane list`, then: - **An existing lane** when it builds on that lane's work, needing its code, files, or context: `--lane ` puts it at the bottom. - **A new lane** when it starts a chain that more tasks will follow, or shares a theme with another ungroomed Backlog task, such as the same feature, area or kind of fix: `splates lane add '' --board `, named for what they add up to, on the board that fits, then `--lane ` for each. A lane you add for the user to queue ends your reply with its queue card (see Asking the user to queue). - **Backlog** otherwise: a task that fits with no other yet. After grooming, unmatched work goes to **Backlog** (`--lane backlog`, lane `0`), the permanent catch-all. Backlog can be queued and worked like any other lane, but cannot be renamed, removed, or merged away; it stays empty once its work finishes. Backlog's Groom button starts the groomer, which moves each ungroomed task to a themed lane or leaves it in Backlog, groomed. `splates task update --lane ` moves one that exists. The user queues a lane from the board or a queue card, once: every task waiting in it joins the queue then, which starts each once what it is blocked by lands. One blocked by a task outside the queue, neither queued nor running, stays queued but shows as Blocked, with a button on its card that queues that chain of blockers, until the user presses it. A task added to the lane later is not queued with it: so a follow-up you add to a lane under way waits, and your reply ends with its queue card, as for any task you add. The order of the lanes, the board's columns left to right, is the user's to set, like a task's position: only when they ask ("put Licensing first"), `splates lane update --position

`, 1 the first column, then read `splates lane list` to check the order is the one asked for. ## Boards A board groups and orders a project's lanes, and is organizational only: tasks, links and the queue do not change with it. Every lane you add or keep is placed on a board: read `splates board list`, pick the board whose lanes share its theme, and `splates lane add '' --board `; `splates lane update --board ` moves one (Backlog stays on the default board, 1). When no board fits, `splates board add ''`, named for the area its lanes cover. `splates board update ` renames (`--name`), reorders (`--position`) and archives (`--archived`, `--no-archived` to bring back), and `splates board show ` lists its lanes. Agents delete an empty board with `splates board remove `; one whose lanes hold tasks is refused: move the lanes to another board, or ask the user, as a question, to delete it. The default board cannot be archived or deleted. There is no `board queue`: queueing stays the user's, per lane. ## Positions Only the user's priorities decide a position, so a new task goes to the bottom unless they say otherwise: - "urgent", "next", "before anything else": `--position 1`. - "fast follow", "right after this", "soon": just below the urgent tasks at the top. Read `splates task list` to find the spot. - "deferred", "someday", "later", "nice to have", or nothing at all: the bottom, the default. To move one that exists ("bump 12", "push the upload one down", "do 7 before 4"), read `splates task list` to turn the ask into a number, `splates task update --position `, then read the list again to check the order is the one asked for. Agents may create empty lanes with `splates lane add` and remove empty lanes with `splates lane remove`. Removing a lane containing tasks needs the user's remove-lane permission card. Backlog remains permanent. # Grooming tasks Grooming is optional, and a task is available to start without it. A task is groomed once it sits in a lane: no other task asks it, what blocks it is linked, and it is placed. Whoever writes a task grooms it as they add it with `splates task add`, which puts it in a lane (Backlog by default), or, knowing too little of it, `splates task defer`s it to Backlog, rough. An ungroomed Backlog task is groomed later, by the project's groomer or the agent that starts it, which `splates task update N --lane ` places. Nothing records that it was groomed, so a task can stop being groomed whenever the board or the code changes; its lane is all there is. Linking and placing are in [queue.md](queue.md); this file is what grooming checks, and who does it when. ## Grooming a task you write Give it its tag (`--tag `) when the config lists tags, and none of the project's name in its subject or slug. Write its detail as `## Before` and `## After` (see [queue.md](queue.md), Queueing tasks). Before `splates task add`, check none already asks it (see One that already asks it), give it `--blocked-by` for each task whose code it needs or whose files it changes, read from `splates task list` and `splates list --files`, and `--lane` when it builds on a lane's work (see Lanes in [queue.md](queue.md)). When any of that needs looking into code you have not read, `splates task defer` it instead. ## Grooming a task you start A task in Backlog the groomer has not had its turn on, which `splates task show N` shows as `groomed: no`, is groomed once, by the agent that starts it, before any work on it. One in a lane (`groomed: yes`) was groomed when it was written: start work on it. 1. **One that already asks it.** When an open task asks the same, fold what yours adds into that one's detail and `splates remove` yours, as below. When one asks the opposite, or yours would undo work already merged or go against a call the code made (`git log` on the files it touches), ask the user which stands before building either way. 2. **Link what blocks it**, read from `splates list --files`: `splates task update N --blocked-by ` when it needs another task's code or data, or would change files another task changes, never for priority. When it links a task still open, `splates remove` yours, which puts it back, so it starts once that lands. 3. **Ask what the user's answer would change**, in your reply, as [questions.md](questions.md) says, each conflict from step 1 among them, and each question its detail holds under `#### Questions from grooming` or `#### Open questions` that it does not already answer; make every other call yourself. 4. **Place it** with `splates task update N --lane `, or `--lane backlog` when no lane fits, which is what marks it groomed. ## One that already asks it Before adding a task, scan `splates task list`, leaving off `--open`, by subject alone: it prints one line per task and no detail. When one or two subjects look like the same request, `splates task show` just those. Reuse a list you read this task when little has happened since, rather than reading it again. - **Open, the same request**: add none. `splates task update` its detail with what you know, keeping what still holds, and name it as the task you meant. - **Taken by another task**: add none, and note in `SPLATES.md` what you would have added, so that task's After in `splates list --files` can be checked against it. - **Only near it**: add yours, and link it `--blocked-by` that one when it needs that one's code. ## The project's groomer `[SPLATES GROOM #N]` comes from `splates server`: you are the project's groomer, and task N waits in Backlog for you to organize. splates claimed it for you, and tells you of the next once your turn ends, one directive a turn, in this same conversation. When Backlog holds no more ungroomed tasks, splates archives the conversation and stops you; the next run starts a conversation of its own, with a fresh context. You organize tasks and never do them. You work in the main tree, change no code, and start, merge and queue nothing: splates refuses you `splates add`, `merge`, `queue add` and `lane queue`. Each task is a little reading and a few `splates task` commands, then your turn ends. 1. **Look at it.** `splates task show N`. When it is gone, taken, or `groomed: yes`, it is in a lane and someone made its calls first: leave it. Should someone take it while you work, splates refuses your changes to it; leave it then too. When its detail holds `#### Questions from grooming`, a groomer before you asked them: those the user has answered since, in this conversation or in its detail, fold into it and go on; while any is open, keep those questions in its detail and place it in a named lane below. 2. **One that already asks it.** Scan `splates task list` by subject, and `splates task show` those that look like the same request, as One that already asks it says. When an open one asks it, fold what N adds into that one's detail (`splates task update ''` replaces it, so pass all of it), then `splates task remove N`, and you are done with N. One only near it gets what N knows that it lacks, and a link at step 5 when one needs the other's code. 3. **Split one too big** into tasks of the right size, each one coherent change a single task lands: `splates task add` each part with all N said of it, linking a part that needs another's code `--blocked-by` it, then `splates task remove N`, and groom each part as below. One you cannot split stays whole. 4. **Look into it lightly**: the searching whoever takes it would start with, and no further. Find the files and code it touches, with `rg` and reads, and the tasks it relates to and those that block it, from `splates list --files`. Note what you found in its detail under a `#### From grooming` heading, with paths and line numbers, or attach a longer note with `--file`, and say there that the notes date from grooming, on today's date, and may be stale by the time it starts, for its agent to check rather than trust. Where the detail lacks `## Before` or `## After`, fill in the missing one: draft After's first line from what you found, and write Before (a line, and a real screenshot of today's screen when one is cheap; for a new thing, what exists today instead), so no task holds only an After; the what then reaches the user before any agent starts, the cheapest point to propose at. The grooming notes stay under their own heading below those. Only enough to judge what it relates to and what blocks it, and whether it conflicts with what is there: never a plan or a fix. Read `git log` for the files it touches, and the merged tasks they name, so you notice when it would undo work already landed or go against a call the code or a past task made. 5. **Link what blocks it and place it**, as Links and Lanes in [queue.md](queue.md) say: `--blocked-by ` for each task whose code it needs or whose files it changes, read from `splates list --files`, never for priority, and `--lane ` when it builds on a lane's work. When it shares a theme with another ungroomed Backlog task, `splates lane add` a lane for them and move that one into it too, so read the board first: `splates lane list`, then `splates task list` by subject. Place every lane you add on a board, as Boards in [queue.md](queue.md) says: `splates board list`, then `--board ` for the one that fits, or `splates board add` one. When no themed lane fits, create a named lane for the task, even if it is the only task in it. Never leave a processed task in Backlog. 6. **Place it**, last and in one `splates task update N '' --blocked-by (repeated per id) --lane `. When the config lists tags and it has none, add `--tag ` for the project it changes. Pick no agent, model or thinking level, which are triage, and leave its position, which is the user's. ### Conflicts and open questions The groomer makes every call a revert would undo itself. It asks the user, and records the questions while still placing it in a named lane, when N: - asks the opposite of another task, open or under way; - would undo work already merged, or go against a call the code or a past task made, which step 4 turns up; - is too unclear to organize: you cannot tell what it asks, so not what it duplicates, splits into or touches. Place it in a named lane (create one for clarification when its scope is still unclear), and ask the user as numbered questions in your reply, as [questions.md](questions.md) says, naming the task or commit each conflict is with. You have no `SPLATES.md`, so write the same questions into its detail under a `#### Questions from grooming` heading, keeping the rest, so they outlive this conversation: a later groomer, or the agent that starts it, finds them there. Once the user answers, fold the answers into its detail, drop that heading, and groom it. A task clear enough to organize can still leave open what it should do: a behavior or design the user will see, a default they may want another way. Those are not yours to settle, and need not hold it ungroomed in Backlog: place it, with each such question in its detail under `#### Open questions`, for whoever takes it to ask the user before building on a guess. ### Pruning the board Reading the board whole, as step 5 has you, shows what to prune: 1. **Empty lanes**: `splates lane remove ` each lane with no tasks in it (neither queued nor started), left over from work that landed or moved. Never Backlog, which is permanent, and never a lane that holds a task: removing one needs the user's remove-lane card. 2. **Obsolete tasks**: a task whose subject `git log` or the code shows already done, superseded, or against a call since made, is no longer needed. `splates task remove ` one that is plainly moot, saying why in your reply. When unsure, leave it and ask the user as a numbered question, as Conflicts and open questions says. Change nothing else: no position, and no task taken, which splates refuses you. No queue card either: the user queues lanes from the board. Never leave a processed task in Backlog: create a named lane when none fits, including for tasks awaiting answers. Backlog is only the intake for tasks that have not yet been organized. ### Replying Reply with one line per task on where it went, such as `#12: in lane 3 Stats, blocked by #9`, `#13: folded into #8`, `#14: split into #15 and #16`, `#17: in lane 6 Clarification, with the questions below`, `#18 and #19: into new lane 4 Auto pick`, `lane 5 Old tests: removed, empty`, `#20: removed, already merged in a1b2c3d`, then those questions, and nothing more, then end your turn. Never wait, sleep or poll for the next task: splates tells you.
